problems.title: Orthogonal output actions do not preserve a fixed margin
problems.source_location: Lemmas 2–3 and Theorem 1, PDF p.5; Appendix A.1, p.19
claim: The paper infers fixed-class margin-gradient norm invariance from norm-preserving input and output representations, even using diagonal output signs in its proof.
analysis: Let \(f(t)=(t,t^2-1)\), input action \(t\mapsto-t\), and output action \(\rho=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\). Exact equivariance and orthogonality hold. Class one is uniquely predicted at both \(t=1/4\) and \(-1/4\), but margin \(m=1+t-t^2\) has derivative norms \(1/2\) and \(3/2\). Independent logit sign changes alter cancellation. General output mixing also invalidates the diagonal-only margin identity: with \(f(x)=x\) and a coordinate swap, the transformed margin at \((2,1)\) is \(-1\), whereas the diagonal expression is zero.
result: The central fixed-margin theorem is false under its explicit hypotheses. Full-Jacobian Euclidean norm invariance under orthogonal multiplication remains correct, but does not supply fixed-class margin invariance.
repair: Require the margin covector \(a=e_c-e_j\) to obey \(a^\top\rho=a^\top\), and the inverse input action to preserve the chosen dual norm. Then \(\nabla m(A_gx)=A_g^{-\top}\nabla m(x)\). Relabel transformed classes consistently when using permutations.
problems.impact_rationale: An exact smooth equivariant classifier contradicts the main orbit-invariant margin theorem while retaining the same predicted class at both inputs.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Local certificate needs a radius cap and a neighborhood supremum
problems.source_location: Definitions 4–5, PDF p.4; Appendix A.1 final equality, p.19
claim: The certificate uses margin divided by a gradient supremum on a local radius-\(r\) ball, without capping the result at \(r\), and replaces an orbit-neighborhood supremum by a center value.
analysis: For \(m(t)=1-t^2,x=0,r=1/10\), the exact local constant is \(1/5\), giving the uncapped ratio \(5\). But \(t=11/10\) has negative margin despite distance below \(5\). Separately, invariant logits \((1+\|x\|^2,0)\) at radius \(1\) have gradient norm \(2\) on their orbit, while the radius-\(1/4\) orbit neighborhood has supremum \(5/2\). Orbit invariance cannot remove the transverse neighborhood.
result: The stated local certificate can exceed the domain where its bound is valid, and the proof’s final supremum equality is false even with invariant logits.
repair: Use strict perturbation radius \[\min\{r,\min_j m_j(x)/L_j(r)\}\]. Under the appropriate scalar-margin/input-isometry hypotheses, local-ball suprema are equal along an orbit, but are not equal to one gradient value.
problems.impact_rationale: A claimed certified radius admits an explicit label-changing perturbation smaller than that radius, invalidating a central guarantee.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Equivariance does not impose directional gradient dominance
problems.source_location: Lemma 5 and Theorem 2, PDF p.6; Appendix A.2, p.20
claim: Theorem 2 asserts that off-orbit perturbations change gradients much more than equal tangent perturbations under compact-group equivariance.
analysis: For rotation-invariant \(F(x)=s-s^2/6,s=\|x\|^2\), use \(x=(1,0)\), tangent perturbation \((0,t)\) and radial perturbation \((t,0)\). The radial gradient change is \((-2t^2-2t^3/3,0)\), while the tangent change is \((-2t^2/3,4t/3-2t^3/3)\). Their norm ratio tends to zero, reversing the asserted ordering. A tangent straight-line displacement need not remain on the orbit, and constant gradient norm does not make gradient vectors equal. For Lemma 5 separately, averaging untransported gradients of \(\|x\|^2\) over \(\{I,-I\}\) gives zero: the difference from the gradient at \((1,0)\) is \(2\), versus only \(2t\) for a small radial perturbation.
result: Both smoothing/directional assertions fail in smooth exact-symmetry examples. Invariance alone supplies no universal ordering or improved robustness magnitude.
repair: Retain only \(\nabla F(x)^\top v=0\) for orbit-tangent \(v\), and pull gradients back by \(A_g^\top\) when differentiating group-averaged values. A directional comparison needs additional Hessian/curvature bounds not provided here.
problems.impact_rationale: A globally smooth invariant polynomial asymptotically reverses the paper’s second main theorem, so this is substantial theoretical damage.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Attack clipping and evaluation mode alter the intended comparison
problems.source_location: Section 6.2, PDF pp.8–9; CIFAR-100 baseline attack functions; fullyeqv/test.py, evaluate_attack
claim: The baseline normalizes pixels to \([-1,1]\) but clips attacks to \([0,1]\); another comparator uses \([-1,1]\). The fully equivariant evaluator switches to training mode while attacking.
analysis: A legal raw pixel \(0.25\) normalizes to \(-0.5\). A zero-budget baseline attack then clamps it to \(0\), moving it by \(0.5\) in normalized units. The fully equivariant preprocessing can map legal pixels to \(-2\), but its clip moves them to \(-1\) even at zero budget. model.train activates training-mode layers and can update batch-normalization buffers; enabling gradients does not require that mode.
result: The current release has inconsistent attack domains and mutable model evaluation state. The exact impact on the published figures and corrected rankings remains unresolved. The fully equivariant changes were previously modified and reverted, so novelty is not asserted.
repair: Attack raw pixels through the composed normalization/model map, or use exact per-channel normalized intervals and budgets. Keep model evaluation mode while enabling autograd, and preserve buffers.
problems.impact_rationale: These are bounded release/protocol defects with unresolved code-to-figure lineage and unmeasured corrected rankings.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Finite scales and a generic head do not establish global equivariance
problems.source_location: Section 4.5, PDF p.7; Appendix C.1.2, pp.21–22; fullyeqv/model.py, lines 35–36 and 51–53
claim: The theory is applied to a finite positive scaling collection and a model with regular-representation features followed by spatial pooling and an unconstrained linear classifier.
analysis: A finite multiplicative subgroup of positive reals must be \(\{1\}\), since finite order implies \(s^n=1\) and hence \(s=1\). The set \(\{0.5,1,2\}\) is not closed because it lacks \(4\). Bilinear down/up-sampling is also noninvertible. Separately, invariant class logits after regular-channel permutation \(P_g\) require \(WP_g=W\). Spatial pooling followed by an ordinary linear head imposes no such condition: \(v=e_1,w^\top=e_1^\top\) gives output \(1\), but a channel shift to \(e_2\) gives zero.
result: The cited implementations do not establish the whole-logit group premises. Symmetry-inspired multiscale and hybrid architectures may still be empirically useful; approximate symmetry is a separate claim.
repair: Describe finite multiscale aggregation as such, or specify an actual group action. Use group pooling or a constrained invariant/intertwining head before invoking the global theorem.
problems.impact_rationale: This is an assumption-to-architecture correspondence issue; no trained model’s measured error or approximate symmetry is numerically refuted.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

impact_rationale: Major: exact counterexamples refute both main symmetry-based robustness theorems and the uncapped local certificate.
